#3532. I Analyzed the Seven Biggest AI Chatbots to Determine How Safe They Are for Kids

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

AI safety for both adults and children is under greater scrutiny than ever before, with a growing number of questions and concerns appearing around how beneficial or otherwise these conversational bots actually are for our mental well-being—even without considering their energy use, ethics, or economic implications. At the same time, an increasing number of apps and services are becoming age-gated in a growing number of countries around the world, as governments realize that letting kids loose on AI apps, social media platforms, and the web at large might not be the best idea for their ongoing development and prosperity.

The big AI apps, such as ChatGPT and Gemini, are right in the center of these trends, and the companies behind them are taking steps that they promise will keep children safe. If you want to know what youngsters in your family may be getting exposed to, and what you can do about it, here's the rundown.

OpenAI's ChatGPT has one of the more comprehensive setups in terms of parental controls. The minimum age for users is 13, and if you're under 18, you need to have parental consent to open an account—age is predicted via several signals, including what times of day you use ChatGPT and what you talk about.

Accounts for under-18s automatically become ChatGPT for Teens accounts. There's more of a focus on learning and study (with a dedicated study mode), as well as "age-appropriate safeguards to help reduce exposure to sensitive or potentially harmful content." There are built-in protections for "harmful topics," including sexual, romantic, or violent roleplay, graphic violence, and self-harm. These work on top of the safeguards for all users that limit chats about physical harm and illegal activity.

These ChatGPT for Teens accounts can also be linked to a parental account—but while parental consent is required for under-18s to use the service, ChatGPT clearly says that teens do have the option to break the link if they want. If you do persuade your kid to keep your accounts connected, you can set time limits on when the AI bot can be used, and tweak some of the sensitivity settings. However, you can't view any conversations.

To set up parental controls from ChatGPT on the web, click your profile icon (bottom left), then Settings > Parental controls > Add family member and follow the instructions. It's also worth bearing in mind that ChatGPT app can also be used for free, anonymously, in any web browser, though OpenAI says users accessing the AI this way are subject to the default under-18s limits (and can't save chats or access an archive).

Gemini is tied into everything else Google does, and follows the broader rules for Google accounts: No under-13s, unless you're part of a family group and using an account managed by an adult. You can manage your family through the Family Link portal on the web, though as far as parental controls specific to Gemini go, you can only enable or disable access to the AI (settings like screen time apply across all enabled apps).

For all under-18s (partly identified through age estimation), whether or not they're part of a managed family group, Google applies some additional protections. They include preventing the AI from taking on a persona, guarding against emotional dependence on the AI, and discouraging bullying and other forms of harassment. There are also safeguards to limit chats about age-restricted substances like alcohol or vapes, and mental health issues like eating disorders.

These protections for minors are applied in addition to the usual guardrails in Gemini for everyone. The guardrails should lead you away from conversations about self-harm, suicide, violence, and illegal activities, and offer quick links to support in times of crisis. However, Google itself admits that these filters aren't perfect.

As with ChatGPT, there's a loophole of sorts in that anyone can start chatting with Gemini, for free inside a web browser, with no checks at all. These conversations can't be saved and come up against usage limits fairly quickly, but they're only protected by the general restrictions for all accounts, not the ones specific to minors.

Meta AI will show up in several apps that young people and children are likely to use, including WhatsApp and Instagram, as well as having its own separate app on the web and on phones. The standard restrictions for Meta's social media accounts apply to its AI too: A minimum age of 13, and restrictions for all under-18s. Like many other platforms, it uses some AI magic to flag up accounts being used by minors.

If you're under 18 and on a Meta Teen account, you'll come up against blocks if you try to get Meta AI to engage in sexual or romantic roleplay, or discuss alcohol or substance misuse. Chats on topics such as eating disorders and self-harm will prompt the AI to offer guidance towards relevant support services.

Meta offers a comprehensive parental control setup for its apps, including Meta AI, but connecting a parent account isn't compulsory for teens. This is handled through the Meta Family Center portal, and parents can get reports on the general topics that kids are chatting about with AI—though they don't get the exact transcripts or prompts. Any self-harm or suicide discussion can trigger an alert to the connected parent account.

All users, under 18 or over 18, get support and crisis intervention responses when chatting about suicide and self-harm, and there are strict limits on discussing illegal and harmful acts, including drug use and cyberbullying, as well as sexual and adult content.

Apple users have to be 13 or over to have an account, which is required to access Siri AI—anyone younger needs to have an account created for them by an adult, and these accounts can only get at the basic, older Siri. Date of birth must be declared when opening an Apple account, with tighter checks rolling out in many parts of the world.

Anyone over the age of 13 can have an Apple account and use the Siri AI app, with or without a connected parent account, as it stands in most U.S. states. This means the well-being safeguards are essentially the same for teens as they are for adults: There are safeguards around self-harm, suicide, sexual and violent content, and illegal commands. It's one of the more conservative AIs when it comes to what it will talk about.

The new and improved Siri AI can be managed to some extent by the new parental controls available in iOS 27 and Apple's other software updates for 2026—Apple has clearly seen the way the wind is blowing—but this is optional for teens. It depends on whether or not you can corral your kids into a Family Sharing group.

If your teens are in your family group of users, then the standard Screen Time rules apply for controlling app usage limits and device access (in iOS Settings, tap your name, then Family to get at them). There are also options for disabling certain Siri AI features, such as the writing tools or the image creation capabilities.

Like Gemini/Google and Apple/Siri, Copilot is tied into the wider Microsoft ecosystem, and access for under-18s can be managed through it. Users must be 13 or older to hold a Microsoft or a Copilot account—and again, there's some underlying tech in place to detect anyone who might be deliberately lying about their age.

If you've got a teen using Copilot, you can manage their access through the standard Microsoft Family Safety portal. You're able to enable or disable Copilot access, set times during which Copilot can and can't be used, and disable certain features like image generation or voice mode. Parents can't read the Copilot chats of their kids, though.

Parental supervision is optional—a teen aged 13–17 can use Copilot without linking their account to an adult one. Microsoft says users identified as under 18 won't see personalized results or ads, and will get age-appropriate responses regarding risky or harmful content, though there's not much detail on what that entails.

More generally, content around self-harm, violence, adult content, harassment, and harmful or illegal activity is banned on the AI platform. Any prompts about suicide or drugs will bring up support options rather than answers, whether you're an adult or a young person using the service.

Out of the bigger AI chatbots out there, Grok is very much the worst at protecting minors. It can be accessed through X or as its own standalone app, and while its terms of use indicate there's a minimum age requirement of 13, a recent report by Common Sense Media says the platform's age checks aren't effective.

Ultimately that means that minors have the same access to Grok as adults, if they want it—an AI platform that combines "weak safety guardrails" and "a range of extremely harmful content" that includes "explicit sexual content, mental health risks, violent content, and inappropriate responses to... offensive content" (that's the Common Sense Media Report again).

Yes, this is the AI chatbot that has previously had a problem with deepfake porn imagery, and which has traditionally taken a rather casual attitude towards safety concerns, led by SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk. While illegal and harmful content is supposedly banned from Grok, its own FAQs admit that certain chats can result in "dialogue that may involve coarse language, crude humor, sexual situations, or violence."

There is actually a Grok Kids Mode that limits the kind of content that can be shown and the conversation topics that can be added, but it requires users to self-declare themselves as minors and is easy to bypass. The advice from Common Sense Media seems to be the way to go with Grok: Do not let your teens access it.

Claude's approach to child safety is straightforward: You can only register for an account if you're over 18. It is possible to lie about your age when signing up, but like the other platforms, Anthropic looks at various "signals" in behavior to spot minors—if your account gets flagged, you have to verify your age using an option like face age estimation or Yoti.

There's no free web access to the chatbot, like there is with ChatGPT and Gemini, so if you're under 18, you're locked out from the service unless you know the behavioral tricks to get past Claude's detection systems.

In terms of more general well-being protections on Claude, any chat around self-harm or suicide will guide users towards helplines and other resources for support. Conversations about illegal activities, disallowed speech, and explicit sexual content are banned from the platform. In recent months, Anthropic says it's also reduced AI sycophancy.

That's something of a whistle-stop tour of the big seven AI chatbots, but if you're a parent, it should give you some idea of what's out there and how easy it is to access. Besides the parental controls built into these AIs (or not), you also have the settings available at the platform level—Android, iOS, Windows, macOS—to restrict the use of any potentially harmful apps.

I've been a fan of “Percy Jackson” for as long as I can remember. I still remember picking up the books for the first time as a kid and getting completely swept up in Rick Riordan’s world of Greek mythology, monsters and teenage demigods. It’s a franchise I’ve had a soft spot for ever since, so seeing it find a new audience through Disney’s adaptation has been a real treat. And now, somehow, we’re already heading into "Percy Jackson and the Olympians" season 3. I can’t quite believe how quickly that’s come around, but I’m certainly not complaining.

Season 3 adapts “The Titan's Curse,” the third book in Riordan’s beloved series. This time, Percy (Walker Scobell) and Grover (Aryan Simhadri) find themselves on a dangerous mission to rescue Annabeth (Leah Sava Jeffries), who has gone missing following an encounter with a mysterious new threat. With the fate of Olympus hanging in the balance, Percy must contend with powerful enemies and a prophecy that could change everything. It’s another big adventure for the young demigods, but one that comes with considerably higher stakes.

I’ve watched the first four episodes of season 3, and there’s plenty to get excited about. While the show still has the humor, friendship and sense of adventure that made me fall in love with the books in the first place, this latest chapter feels noticeably more mature. It’s an encouraging step forward for the Disney+ series, and one that makes me even more invested in seeing where these characters go next. Here’s what I thought of the first four episodes.

I’m Alix, a lifelong horror nerd who loves watching, reviewing and writing about the latest movies and TV shows. When I’m not working through my ever-growing horror watchlist, I’m covering the biggest releases across streaming and film, including "VisionQuest" on Disney+, "The Institute" season 2 on MGM+, and "Guarding Stars" on Netflix.

Season 3 of “Percy Jackson and the Olympians” wastes little time setting a darker, more action-packed tone. It opens with Thalia Grace (Tamara Smart) hunting for Luke (Charlie Bushnell) in a parking garage, where she finds herself battling a dangerous monster. Percy soon crashes into the fight. Thalia isn’t particularly thrilled about needing his help, which establishes some immediate friction between the two demigods. The opening also introduces the season’s central mission, with Annabeth explaining that she needs Thalia’s help to rescue two young demigods, siblings Nico (Levi Chrisopulos) and Bianca di Angelo (Olive Abercrombie).

Book readers will understand the significance of these characters straight away, while show-only viewers will get a better idea as the season unfolds. Thankfully, the first episode doesn't take long to get the main story moving, either, as Annabeth is abducted, triggering Percy’s fatal flaw: his unwavering loyalty. He’s determined to get her back, no matter how dangerous the quest becomes. That sense of danger carries through the first four episodes, and I think it’s one of the season’s biggest improvements.

With the group getting older and the looming threat of war becoming increasingly difficult to ignore, the show feels noticeably more mature in its storytelling. Percy and his friends are exposed to greater dangers, and there’s a stronger sense that their actions could have serious consequences. It’s also great to see the series developing Percy’s abilities, particularly his control over water. His powers have felt somewhat underexplored in previous seasons, so watching him become more confident and capable with them is a welcome change. He’s clearly getting stronger, and I hope the remaining episodes continue to build on that.

Of course, you can't talk about “Percy Jackson” without mentioning Percabeth, and I know plenty of fans are just as invested in Percy and Annabeth’s developing relationship as they are in the Greek mythology. Thankfully, season 3 gives us a little more to enjoy on that front. It’s still very much a slow burn, with neither quite ready to acknowledge that their feelings might be more than friendship, but there’s a growing awareness that something special is there. The dance scene in episode 1 is a particularly lovely example of this. I suspect season 3 will give Percabeth fans plenty to get excited about.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Based on the first four episodes, season 3 is probably the strongest “Percy Jackson” season yet. I particularly appreciate is how much more attention is given to the emotional baggage these teenagers carry as the children of some incredibly powerful figures, many of whom seem largely uninterested in their own kids’ lives. including Thalia’s complicated relationship with Zeus. We get more of an insight into how these circumstances fuel their trauma and motives.

It gives the series a little more emotional depth without losing sight of the fun. The visual effects are also stronger, with the action sequences feeling grander and more cinematic than before. There’s a real sense that the show is becoming more ambitious with each season, and these early episodes have me excited to see what’s next. If the remaining episodes maintain this momentum, “Percy Jackson” could reach a whole new level, and I can only hope Disney+ has more seasons covering the rest of the books in store.

The first two episodes of "Percy Jackson" season 3 is streaming on Disney+, with the final six episodes releasing in pairs every Friday through December 11, 2026.

#3529. How to Check Your Flight Status After the FAA Canceled the Ground Stop for All Airports

Update, 8:41 p.m.: The Federal Aviation Administration announced it has ended the ground stop.

On Friday afternoon, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop for all airports in the United States. If you're planning to fly this afternoon or evening, or you have friends or family doing the same, you're likely concerned about tracking flight statuses. While there's still a lot we don't know, there are tools to help track flights at this time:

There are a number of options for tracking flights, whether you have your flight number or not. If you have the flight number, the fastest method is to Google it: Google will display a live tracker of your flight at the top of the results page. You can also head to the airline's official website to track your flight: United Airlines, for example, has a flight tracker where you can either enter your route information or your flight number. Most, if not all, airlines will have a similar tool you can use.

Alternatively, you can use a site or service that tracks all flights. FlightAware is one such site and has a flight tracker that lets you search flights—so long as you know the origin and the destination. If you have the flight number, your iPhone can help: You can enter your flight number into Spotlight search to see a live tracker, or you can text a contact your flight number, then tap the link that appears under the number to see a tracker of the flight.

At this time, the exact reason isn't totally clear. According to the agency, “The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” but the FAA hasn't said what caused those communications issues or when they expect to lift the grounding. The grounding order comes one day after a massive Microsoft outage that disrupted service for users of Outlook, Teams, and other Microsoft products. It also comes one day after Ars Technica reported that the FAA was rolling out an AI-powered tool to help manage air traffic across the country.

This is only the third time in U.S. history that the FAA has made such an order—once after 9/11, and again in January of 2023 due to a pilot alert system issue; the latter ground stop lasted around 90 minutes.

#3528. New John Carpenter Meets The Terminator Thriller Confirms HBO Max Release Date

The new action thriller Onslaught is coming to HBO Max next month, and the release date has just been announced.

Onslaught was released in theaters this September and grossed $3.5 million at the box office. In the film, an Army sniper springs into action after genetically engineered super soldiers go rogue. Celeste Cross, the sniper, has a lot at stake as she has a young child to protect, and she will do whatever it takes to ensure her daughter's safety.

The film, which has been described as John Carpenter meets The Terminator, will arrive on HBO Max on December 22. This comes after Onslaught was released on digital platforms in early October.

December will also see several other films be added to HBO Max, including Bad Times at the El Royale, BlacKkKlansman, the Rocky and Creed franchise, Free Willy, The Goonies, Mamma Mia! Here We Go Again, Matilda, Meet the Parents, Mrs. Doubtfire and Alien: Romulus, along with the original series My Favorite Murder, C.B. Strike and Harry Potter.

Adria Arjona plays Celeste Cross in Onslaught, which also stars Dan Stevens, Eric Wareheim, Reginald VelJohnson, Michael Biehn, Alex Pereira, Drew Starkey and Rebecca Hall.

Simon Barrett wrote the script for the film, which takes place in the same universe as Wingard's 2014 thriller The Guest. The director and screenwriter also served as producers with Aaron Ryder, Andrew Swett, Jeremy Platt and Alexander Black.

Aside from having an underwhelming box office return, Onslaught received mixed-to-positive reviews from critics, who gave it a 59% on Rotten Tomatoes. (The audience score is virtually the same at 60%.)

Reviewers claimed the film relied on too many clichés with an incoherent premise. On the other hand, some of the more positive reviews called Onslaught intriguing, entertaining and intense, and praised Arjona's performance.

ScreenRant's Brandon Zachary reviewed Onslaught and gave it a 7 out of 10.

Onslaught is one of A24's more recent films, alongside other 2025 releases like The Drama, Mother Mary, Backrooms, Tony, Primetime and the hit documentary You Can See Everything about Elizabeth Holmes.

Before Onslaught, Wingard had directed the blockbusters Godzilla vs. Kong and Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire, which grossed $470 million and $572 million, respectively. He decided not to return for the upcoming Godzilla x Kong: Supernova in order to direct Onslaught. Wingard has also helmed Blair Witch, Death Note and You're Next, among other projects.

Onslaught will be released on HBO Max on Tuesday, December 22, 2026.

#3525. New Home Alone Movie Officially in Development With Macaulay Culkin Returning

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

Kevin McCallister got left behind in Illinois, then lost in New York, and somehow Macaulay Culkin made both look like pretty appealing ways to spend Christmas. He could order his own pizza, charge an unreasonable amount of room service to his father’s credit card, and make two burglars regret every decision that brought them to his door. The obvious question for another Home Alone movie is what happens when Kevin becomes the adult somebody else wants out of the house.

Culkin has recently been playing Kevin again for McDonald’s holiday campaign, and he told Collider's Hannah Hunt there’s one thing the character would never grow out of: “Defying authority," he said, pointing to the rebellious streak that makes Kevin so easy for kids to root for. Culkin figures adults still understand the appeal of getting one over on somebody bigger, too, because no matter how old you are, “You always have a boss."

A new Home Alone movie with Culkin is now in development at Disney, according to new reports. Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg have reportedly closed a deal to produce through Point Grey and will work with Culkin to develop the script. Disney declined to comment on the report, so as of now there’s no release date attached, but the reported deal gives Kevin’s potential movie comeback a strong producing team.

Culkin spoke with Collider earlier this month about returning as Kevin for McDonald’s, and he sounded happy to have another reason to revisit the character. He described Home Alone as a “wonderful sandbox to play around in,” particularly now that he gets to see people who grew up with the movie introduce it to another generation. “It’s taken on its own life,” he said. That becomes especially obvious whenever November rolls around. Culkin estimates he gets recognized ten times more between November and January, joking that he “cornered the fourth quarter market.”

At screenings now, he gets to watch an audience arrive with years of Christmas memories attached to the movie. “They bring their nostalgia with them,” he told Collider. For those viewers, seeing Kevin again comes with the memory of being a kid who thought having an entire house to themselves sounded like the best present imaginable. For now, Culkin’s latest return is the McDonald’s campaign, which he described as a natural fit for a movie families revisit every year. “The actual food and the movie are comfort food, really,” he said.

A new movie would give those families something they haven’t had since Home Alone 2: Lost in New York in 1992: a Christmas movie with Culkin’s Kevin where they don’t already know what happens next. Stay tuned to Collider for updates on the next Home Alone movie.

#3524. Google Killed Its Dark Web Report, but You Can Still Monitor Data Breaches

Google’s Dark Web Report used to be the only consumer-focused platform that let users scan major data breaches, dark web marketplaces, and private forums to see if their personal information had ended up in the hands of hackers. But the company discontinued the service at the start of 2026, with new scans stopping on Jan. 15 and all accounts deleted on Feb. 16.

Google says it sunsetted Dark Web Report because, although the information it provided was generally useful, the service failed to provide “helpful next steps” for users whose data was found on the dark web. Google promised a new service that would provide more actionable intel, but that service has yet to materialize, and there haven’t been any further announcements about it yet.

Dark Web Report may not have been perfect, but it was the only early warning system of its kind that was available for personal use and let users run scans free of cost. Now that it’s gone, however, there are plenty of other services that offer the same service at varying costs and levels of effectiveness. Let’s talk through the nature of the insight that Google's reports offered, how it collected that information in the first place, and what options exist in the market to replace it.

Google launched the Dark Web Report in March 2023 as a premium feature available to Google One users, but later extended it for free to anyone with a Google account and moved it to the "Results about you" dashboard.

You'd set up a monitoring profile with your name, date of birth, physical address, phone number, emails, and Social Security Number if you lived in the U.S. After that, you could head to the dashboard anytime you wanted to run a free scan across dark web forums and marketplaces, publicly disclosed corporate data breaches, and other hidden online spaces to see if any of your personal information had shown up there. It was easy to use—but not a lot of people knew it existed in the first place.

It’s unclear what prompted the internal decision at Google, but in the absence of concrete next steps, it is reasonable to think the reports could create panic for the uninitiated. There’s no way to remove your information from the dark web once it’s already in circulation there. Still, having an early warning so you could reset 2FA or self-lock your SSN isn’t without merit.

But perhaps more importantly, most people with Google accounts didn’t know and hadn’t heard of the Dark Web Report’s existence. Google has likely taken it as a hint that users want more active remediation tools than simple alerts, which is why it’s now directing users to the Password Manager, Passkeys, and “Results about you” dashboard instead—though, again, the company hasn't followed through on a direct replacement for Dark Web Report, despite teasing such a feature.

Many of the top dark web scanners draw from the same well of information, scanning against major data breaches and dark web spaces. Several also offer breach notifications that send you email alerts when your details show up in a periodic scan. However, none of that is worth paying for because Have I Been Pwned or Mozilla Monitor cover those features quite well for free. Even the default password managers from Google and Apple come with some ability to monitor leaked credentials.

There isn’t an easy way to scrub your information from the dark web once it ends up getting leaked. But you can take steps to protect sensitive information or financial data once you know there’s been a leak. If a password has been compromised, reset it immediately. Also, enable 2FA on the affected account for added security. Even better, switch to a passkey if that account supports it. If not, authenticator apps are a safer way to receive 2FA codes than standard SMS.

If your Social Security number has been leaked, freeze your credit with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. You can do this by contacting each agency separately. Freezing your credit will prevent unauthorized credit withdrawals and protect your credit score from abuse by attackers. If one of your credit or debit card numbers has ended up in a breach, call your bank to freeze transactions on that card immediately.

Finally, get in the habit of using email aliases instead of sharing your actual email address with every platform and service provider. Addy.io and Proton’s SimpleLogin are both popular services that let you generate temporary email aliases that point to your inbox.

#3523. Netflix's Hit 8-Part Psychological Thriller Ignites Cancellation Petition With Over 135K Signatures

Netflix's hit new series has ignited a petition with over 135,000 signatures calling for its cancellation.

This is far from the first instance of a controversial Netflix series. In 2019, the Brazilian comedy, The First Temptation of Christ (2019), sparked protests and petitions claiming blasphemy. In 2020, the French drama Cuties sparked backlash and petitions claiming it sexualized young girls. In 2021, Netflix's own employees protested outside the company's headquarters, claiming that Dave Chappelle's comedy special, The Closer, was transphobic.

Now, over 135,000 people have signed an online petition calling for the cancellation of Netflix's new show, The Body, calling it "blasphemous" and "anti-Christian." The show follows a group of Catholic schoolgirls who perform a mock Satanic ritual, jokingly offering one of their classmates as a virgin sacrifice. After she falls into a coma, they begin having prophetic visions of her, triggering mass hysteria.

The petition, on CitizenGO, calls the show "a blasphemous anti-Christian series featuring satanic ritual," and warns, "Parents cannot screen every show teens press play on. Netflix is counting on that." The petition was launched ahead of the show's debut on November 11, urging Netflix to scrap its release. Now, at the time of writing, the petition has surpassed 135,000 signatures.

Talking to Decider, Marcel Ruiz, who appears in a recurring role as Tyler Flores, reacted to the viral petition, saying the backlash may actually be a sign the show is striking a nerve and tackling issues people care about. Whether audiences are watching because of outrage or curiosity, it's helping the show climb the charts. Despite calls for cancellation, the cast is hoping for The Body season 2. Read Ruiz's full comments below:

I wonder if all of those people that have signed the petition have seen the show? That’s like, something I wonder. And also, in a way, it doesn’t surprise me, not because the show is disrespectful, or because the show deserves to have a petition like that, but that’s sometimes art. I did hear a funny story; my dad told me that this friend of his told him that in his daughter’s private Catholic school, they were telling the kids not to watch it. And I thought, "That’s such a flex." I loved hearing that.

Sometimes, things that are moving the ball forward are also going to have some pushback in some areas. You can’t please everyone at the end of the day, I think. It’s good enough that the show is number one on Netflix. Can’t ask for much else.

We’re waiting by the phone. What was so cool is when we were shooting Season 1, you can’t help yourself but think of a future for these characters and ideas. And I remember the day that I wrapped, I went home and I was so emotional that it was over that I just went on my phone and started writing ideas for Tyler for Season 2. Just like as a way to cope and like have some closure. Definitely, I’m excited to, when the time comes, be able to pick that back up.

Ruiz is right in the sense that The Body debuted at No. 2 on Netflix's Top 10 shows in the United States and No. 3 globally, receiving 5.1 million views and 37.4 million hours viewed worldwide for the week of November 9–15. As of today, November 20, The Body is the No. 1 show on Netflix, both worldwide and in the United States.

Despite the backlash, The Body reviews have been mostly positive from both critics and audiences, resulting in 87% and 96% Rotten Tomatoes scores from those groups, respectively. Critics claim The Body blends religious guilt, teenage angst, striking visuals, and vibrant storytelling into an unapologetically bold and queer coming-of-age tale that constantly defies expectations.

Despite public backlash, streaming services seldom cave to demands to pull titles from their platforms, so it's unlikely to happen to The Body, especially given its success.

#3520. Four Things You Can Do With Google Maps' New 'Ask Maps' Feature

Google has given its AI-powered "Ask Maps" feature a major upgrade, adding tools for trip planning, real-time route guidance, appointment finding, and saved-list search. The updates begin rolling out today on Android and iOS.

Google launched Ask Maps last March as an AI assistant designed to handle questions and requests more complicated than simply searching the word "bar" or "groceries." Instead of performing simple keyword searches, the idea behind Ask Maps is that you can describe several specific requirements at once, and Maps will find places that match them all. For example, you could ask for a restaurant with outdoor seating for a certain number of people, and "Ask Maps" will factor in your past searches and give you results. Of course, AI assistants have a habit of making things up, so even with today's roll-out, you'll want to double-check your sources before you drive an hour to the wrong restaurant.

To me, this is the most useful new feature launching today. Whether you're planning a day trip for holiday shopping or something more ambitious, like a three-day road trip with coastal hikes and oceanfront dining, Ask Maps will put together a day-by-day schedule. Each plan includes insider tips and numbered map pins for every stop, so you can see the whole route at a glance. Once you're happy with the plan, you can share it with friends and family or export it to Google Docs on desktop.

When it's time to head out, you can ask Maps to pull up your itinerary, or look for the "itinerary" badge in your chat history. You'll see real-time details such as live traffic conditions, whether a place is currently open, and even the vibe at your next stop.

Plans can change on the fly, too. Ask Maps to add a scenic viewpoint or a lunch spot along the way, then tap to get directions to your next stop straight from the itinerary.

Here's what else you can use Ask Maps to do, starting today.

Pulling up directions now surfaces "Know Before You Go" tips for your route. These include where to park or charge your car, along with real-time conditions like weather, potential delays, and tolls.

Ask Maps is also gaining some agentic capabilities. Allegedly, you can just ask, “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me,” and Ask Maps will show you open slots across nearby businesses. In addition to finding appointments, Google says this agent will be able to call local businesses on your behalf—stay tuned while I wait for the upgrade and test this one out myself.

If you keep lists of saved places, Ask Maps can now search them for you. Ask something like, "Which spots saved in my lists have availability for 5 in the next 30 minutes?" Ask Maps looks across your lists and checks live availability, so you can pick a place and go.

These updates start rolling out today on Android and iOS. Travel itineraries and saved-list search are available everywhere Ask Maps is offered. "Know Before You Go" route tips and appointment finding are launching first in the U.S., with more regions coming soon.

#3518. Wednesday Season 3 Is Finally Adapting The Real Addams Family

Things are changing for Wednesday, as Jenna Ortega's hit Netflix show leaves Nevermore Academy behind in its upcoming third season. When it debuted in 2022, Wednesday was introduced as a coming-of-age whodunit that followed the titular heroine's supernatural investigation at Nevermore Academy and in the small town of Jericho. Season 1 saw Wednesday trying to adjust to her new school while investigating a string of murders caused by a Hyde monster. Meanwhile, in season 2, the teenage detective faced new threats involving a vision about Enid's death and a conspiracy about a psychiatric hospital.

Wednesday season 3 will be very different from previous installments, with Ortega's character embarking on new misadventures that will take her far beyond Nevermore Academy. Audiences last saw Wednesday tracking down clues that will lead her to Enid's whereabouts. Ahead of its expected 2027 premiere, Wednesday season 3 has already finished filming in Ireland and Paris. Ortega will reprise her leading role, along with Emma Myers as Enid Sinclair, Catherine Zeta-Jones as Morticia Addams, Luis Guzmán as Gomez Addams, Isaac Ordonez as Pugsley Addams, Fred Armisen as Uncle Fester, and Victor Dorobantu as Thing.

While fans will see Wednesday prioritize the search for Enid in the upcoming season, the Addams family will also drive one major storyline. Though Wednesday wasn't created to center the iconic family, Morticia, Gomez, Pugsley, Thing, and Uncle Fester still had key supporting roles throughout the show's first two seasons. Now, fans will get to see much more of them in the next installment, as the series explores buried family secrets that may put Wednesday in danger.

Wednesday season 2 ends with the shocking revelation that Morticia's missing sister, Ophelia, is actually alive and locked away in an underground basement cell at Grandmama Hester Frump's mansion. The cliffhanger also comes with an ominous warning, showing Ophelia writing "Wednesday must die" in blood on the wall of her cell. This effectively sets the stage for the Addams family to take on a much bigger role in season 3, as deeper family secrets finally unfold into the main narrative.

Before the season 2 finale reveal, Ophelia was introduced as Morticia's sister, who lost control of her extraordinary psychic abilities as a student at Nevermore. After her descent into madness, she supposedly went missing after being admitted to the Willow Hill Psychiatric Hospital. Throughout season 2, Ophelia served as a cautionary tale for Wednesday because of their similar psychic powers, with Morticia worrying that her daughter might suffer the same tragic fate because of Wednesday's tendency to overuse her gift for the sake of her investigations.

The character of Wednesday Addams has come a long way over the years, and each actor has brought something special to the iconic Addams Family role.

Fans will learn more about Aunt Ophelia in Wednesday season 3 with the arrival of Casino Royale star Eva Green, who has signed on to play the mysterious character. In addition to her casting, Joanna Lumley has been promoted to series regular in the next installment, following her commanding performance in season 2 as the fabulously wealthy and ruthless Hester Frump. Season 3 will likely see Wednesday trying to uncover why Ophelia was imprisoned. It remains to be seen how this revelation will affect Wednesday's relationship with her grandmother, especially since Hester has openly favored her.

As for Ophelia, it's unclear whether she'll be an enemy or an ally for Wednesday in the upcoming third season. Her chilling message in the season 2 finale could be an attempt to warn her niece about a much greater supernatural threat coming her way. However, if Green's character becomes the antagonist, an intense psychic clash will be inevitable.

As the extended Addams family becomes the central focus of the show's next mystery, Wednesday season 3 finally trades the high school whodunit formula for a multi-generational family thriller. This genre shift will bring the Netflix adaptation back to the franchise's roots. While Ortega's teen detective remains the lead, season 3 promises a full-blown gothic family saga in line with Charles Addams' original cartoon comics and 1960s sitcom, where the macabre clan is placed right at the heart of the story.

Even though the high school element gave the franchise a refreshing new look at the beloved character, Wednesday season 3's genre change will raise the stakes for the titular protagonist more than ever. Ophelia's impending arrival will throw the Addams Family into chaos, as loyalty gets tested and long-buried secrets threaten to further fracture relationships. This will be Wednesday's biggest challenge yet.

Wednesday season 3 is expected to premiere on Netflix in 2027.

Wednesday follows the journey of Wednesday Addams as she attends Nevermore Academy, a boarding school for outcasts. Tasked with mastering her psychic abilities, she confronts a series of town murders and a haunting family mystery from 25 years ago, all while managing new social dynamics.

#3517. 10 Shows Like 'Youth' You Should Watch Next

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Sharon Horgan had a string of British hits (including a couple we'll talk about here), before scoring stated successes with Divorce, Shining Vale, and Bad Sisters. She's quickly rising in the ranks of TV super-producers, the acerbically funny HBO Max rom-com Youth (in which she also stars) being just the latest.

This earlier series created by and starring Sharon Horgan is a family sitcom that feels far more believable than most, seeing Irish primary school teacher Sharon (Horgan) hooking up with American ad exec Rob (Rob Delaney) over the course of a week, only to discover that she's pregnant once he returns home. They don't really have feelings for each other, but decide to give it a go at being a couple, eventually falling into marriage just before the birth of their child. There are lots of jokes and plenty of acerbic dialogue, but this isn't Married... with Children. Sharon and Rob can be a bit nasty to each other and to their sloppy friend group, but there's also something rather sweet in the show's conviction that having someone to be a mess with can be one of life's great joys. Stream Catastrophe on Prime Video.

A little more of a high-concept here, but nevertheless an effective show about reimagining yourself in middle age. Younger follows Liza Miller (Sutton Foster), a recently divorced woman in her 40s who finds that age is a barrier to reentering the publishing industry she left years earlier. After a compliment convinces her that she could pass for a younger woman (poor thing), she manages to convince the right people that she's just 26 in order to land an entry-level job. Seven seasons of misadventures ensue, but much of the show revolves around the twisty-turny relationship between Liza and Josh (Nico Tortorella), a tattoo artist in his twenties. Stream Younger on Netflix.

Bridget Everett stars as Sam Miller, who struggles to find her new direction after moving back to her hometown to care for her dying sister. (Don't worry: There's plenty of comedy in the drama, and it's not as heavy as it sounds.) She's solidly middle-aged and starting over, kinda—making new friends in a familiar environment where she has to confront the past and the future alike. Luckily, her love of singing—and a community of goofy oddballs—are there to help. It's another story of a person of a certain age, trying to rebuild their life following an upheaval. Stream Somebody Somewhere on HBO Max.

When all else fails: Start a punk band. This drama from Sally Wainwright (Gentleman Jack) sees five women start a punk band as a lark, just a fun way to kill some time by entering a local talent context. The women realize very quickly, though, that they're very, very pissed off—about the workplace for women, menopause, a diminished dating pool, caring for aging parents and grown children—all of it tied up in the ways in which we treat women, and particularly middle-aged women. The band is a way to reclaim their voices, which doesn't erase or negate any of their problems nor drama (and there's plenty here), but gives them a platform with which to make some noise about it. Stream Riot Women on Britbox.

More of a traditional sitcom, not that there's anything wrong with that, this one builds a lot of goodwill with the performance of Leanne Morgan, its lead and co-creator (alongside Susan McMartin and Chuck Lorre). She plays the show's lead: a Knoxville, Tennessee wife and mom, who finds herself suddenly single in her 50s after her husband of 33 years leaves her. It's a genial, old-school hang-out show with a phenomenal veteran supporting cast that includes Kristen Johnston, Ryan Stiles, and Tim Daly. Stream Leanne on Netflix.

Michele Buteau, who also co-created the series) stars here as a fashion-forward stylist who'd devoted herself to the wrong guy for way too long. As the series opens, Mavis Beaumont is ready for a fresh start, putting herself and her career first—which does not preclude falling into a number of romantic entanglements. As she says more than once, she's going to take on the fashion world with a "body-positive attitude, cute v-neck, and some lip-gloss." Stream Survival of the Thickest on Netflix.

Certainly the goofiest take here on the idea of starting over in mid-life, this is very much a traditional three-camera sitcom, albeit one with a stacked cast of TV legends. Writer Melanie (Valerie Bertinelli), beautician Joy (Jane Leeves), and soap diva Victoria (Wendie Malick) wind up spending a wild night in Cleveland after a plane to Paris is diverted, discovering in the process that, while they're seen as over-the-hill back in Los Angeles, they're all Ohio 10s—though the sassy caretaker of their house, Elka (Betty White), might not agree. Stream Hot in Cleveland on Paramount+.

She'a s hair younger than Alex, but Fleabag (she's only ever referred to as "Fleabag") is trying to rebuild her life after a bad breakup, with extremely mixed results. This very dark comedy-drama follows a free-spirited, deeply angry single young woman living in London and sharing her romantic ups and downs via confessional asides to us, the audience. She falls, rather reluctantly, for "The Priest" (Andrew Scott)—while she's a confirmed atheist, and he's obviously not, the show doesn't turn aside from the general messiness of the situation. Phoebe Waller-Bridge won separate Emmys as the star, creator, and writer of the series. Stream Fleabag on Prime Video.

Maisel was one of Prime’s first truly buzzy original series, a comedy-drama from Amy Sherman-Palladino (Gilmore Girls) about the title’s Midge Maisel (Rachel Brosnahan), a long-time New York housewife of the late 1950s who discovers a talent for stand-up comedy. Inspired by the real-life careers of comedians like Totie Fields and Joan Rivers, the show is warm and welcoming, with great performances and dialogue; it also achieves something rare in being a show about comedy that’s actually funny. Stream The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel on Prime Video.

The big life change in this earlier Sharon Horgan hit is a little different: Julia Johnstone's mother had been a big help in taking care of Julia's children, but she's not going to do it anymore, leaving this working mom (Anna Maxwell Martin) to take the full brunt of childcare for the first time (her husband in the picture, but not much use). She joins up with other working moms involved with a local support group, including shallow Amanda (Lucy Punch), star of her own ongoing spin-off. Stream Motherland on Prime Video and Britbox.

#3516. 10 Best Low Fantasy Animated Movies, Ranked

It was American author Lloyd Alexander who's credited with coining the term "high fantasy" in his 1971 essay High Fantasy and Heroic Romance, while "low fantasy" appeared later in the 20th century as a contrasting classification. Where high fantasy tells stories set in secondary worlds with their own unique set of rules, low fantasy finds the genre's magical and supernatural elements intrude into our own world—or a setting very heavily based on it.

Though live-action cinema has produced several exceptional low fantasy masterpieces over the years, there's something special about the way animation allows low fantasy filmmakers to really let their imaginations fly. From anime gems like My Neighbor Totoro to modern American blockbusters like How to Train Your Dragon, these are films which show why animation is such a perfect vehicle for low fantasy storytelling.

A girl under an umbrella stands next to Totoro in the rain at a bus stop in Studio Ghibli's My Neighbor Totoro.

A girl under an umbrella stands next to Totoro in the rain at a bus stop in Studio Ghibli's My Neighbor Totoro.

The 1980s saw the birth of Studio Ghibli, the studio that quickly became the quintessential spearhead of anime filmmaking—a title they most definitely still hold. One of their earliest masterworks was Hayao Miyazaki's My Neighbor Totoro, about two young sisters who move with their dad to the Japanese countryside to be closer to their ill mother, where they find comfort and wonder in the company of the forest's friendly spirits.

It's one of the best family movies in film history, a testament to the timeless power of slice-of-life low fantasy. Ma is a Japanese artistic concept defined by intentional emptiness or stillness, and My Neighbor Totoro is a masterful example of ma-heavy filmmaking. But though it's simple, it's also emotionally impactful beyond description, still a must-see for families everywhere nearly 40 years after its release.

Director Henry Selick met author Neil Gaiman just as he was finishing his children's novella Coraline, and since Gaiman was such a fan of Selick's The Nightmare Before Christmas, he invited him to make a film adaptation of Coraline. It's the story of the titular girl, who discovers a secret door in her new home leading to an idealized parallel world that's actually far more sinister than it initially seems.

Coraline was stop-motion animation studio Laika's first-ever feature film (and the only one they've ever made that has been profitable), and what an introduction to such a marvelous studio this was. It's one of the best dark fantasy movies ever made, and even though portal fantasy often makes it tricky to distinguish between high and low fantasy, Coraline's idealized parallel world makes this a clear example of one of the 2000s' best low fantasy gems.

Based on their trilogy of stop-motion-animated documentary short films, Dean Fleischer Camp and Jenny Slate made Marcel the Shell With Shoes On, with Camp directing and Slate voicing the titular one-inch-tall seashell. This is his story, as he and his grandmother search for their missing family after a documentary filmmaker's online videos turn Marcel into an overnight Internet sensation.

One of the most emotional animated movies in recent memory, Marcel the Shell is a beautiful tale about grief, community, and finding wonder in everyday life. It's silly, it's simple, it's funny, yet it's more than emotionally complex enough to satisfy even the most cynical of grown-up viewers. Blending live-action and animation has always resulted in really interesting projects, and as far as the last decade goes, this is probably the best of the bunch.

Irish animation studio Cartoon Saloon have been making some of the fantasy movies with the best lore for years, all thanks to their stories often being heavily inspired by Irish folklore. Case in point: Tomm Moore's Song of the Sea, about a young boy and his mute selkie sister journeying across a fading world to return home after their mother vanishes into the sea.

For one, the colorful visuals are absolutely gorgeous, more than enough to remind anyone of why it's still important to have 2D-animated features in modern times. Add to that a beautiful story, an airtight plot that's perfectly paced from start to finish, and deeply memorable characters, and there should be no question left as to why this is one of the most universally beloved low fantasy films of the 2010s, animated or otherwise.

As if any more proof were needed that Cartoon Saloon is one of the most interesting animation studios currently in operation, there's also Wolkfwalkers, one of the best fantasy films of the 2020s so far. Set in 1650s Ireland, it follows a young English apprentice hunter who befriends a wild native girl from a mystical tribe of wolf-spirits, being pulled into the magical world of the very creatures her father has been ordered to exterminate.

Stories about forbidden friendship in children's animation are aplenty, but what makes Wolfwalkers so special is the gorgeous animation, the deep low fantasy world-building, and the deeply moving father-daughter dynamic that often serves as the film's beating heart. A potent critique of colonialism, authoritarianism, and ecological destruction, this is a must-see for anyone who loves modern animation.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

Toy Story completely revolutionized the film industry by introducing the world to fully CG-animated feature filmmaking, and Toy Story 2 somehow managed to be even better. It's Toy Story 3, however, that many still recognize as Pixar's best film to date. In it, Andy's toys are accidentally sent to a daycare center as he prepares to leave for college, forcing them to decide whether to stay together or fight their way back home.

From the phenomenal character writing to the deep themes to one of the most perfect movie endings of the 2010s, pretty much everything about Toy Story 3 is low fantasy animation perfection. Toys being alive is the only high-concept premise that makes this franchise low fantasy, and Toy Story 3 takes that premise to unprecedentedly ambitious and emotional heights.

It's not all Miyazaki: Studio Ghibli has also made films directed by other filmmakers who are just as talented, perhaps the most talented of whom was the great Isao Takahata. His final film as director was Ghibli's The Tale of the Princess Kaguya, an adaptation of the 10th-century Japanese story The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter. In it, a rapidly-growing child is found inside a bamboo stalk and raised by a humble cutter, eventually thrust into high society as a noble princess.

Princess Kaguya is not only one of Ghibli's greatest films to date, but also one of the best fantasy movie masterpieces of the last 15 years. With its wonderfully unique watercolor animation and its profound emotional and thematic maturity, this is both a fantasy masterpiece and a gorgeous period piece. It's complex, it's deeply moving, and it may just have the most unforgettable ending in Ghibli's entire filmography.

Based on the series of children's books by Cressida Cowell, How to Train Your Dragon gave birth to one of the best fantasy movie trilogies of all time. It tells the story of the awkward young Viking Hiccup, who lives on a dragon-raiding island and befriends a wounded dragon that challenges his tribe's traditions. What ensues is further proof that, though abundant, low fantasy stories of forbidden friendship are genuinely special.

Dragons have always been prevalent across both high and low fantasy stories even before cinema was a thing, but few dragon-centric fantasy films have ever been quite as universally beloved as How to Train Your Dragon. That's for good reason. With Roger Deakins as a consultant and DreamWorks' phenomenal team, the animation is obviously fantastic; but what really makes this stand out as one of the studio's best animated films is the emotional story, the tight plotting, and the excellent character work.

Brad Bird's Ratatouille is many people's favorite Pixar film to date, and it isn't the least bit difficult to see why. Visually wonderful, tonally complex, and emotionally and thematically mature, it tells the engrossing story of a Paris rate with an extraordinary palate, who teams up with a clumsy kitchen garbage boy to secretly become a master chef at a prestigious restaurant.

It's a silly premise that any lesser filmmaker or animation studio may have turned into an equally silly comedy, but Bird treats the premise with such beautiful and sincere earnestness that Ratatouille quickly becomes one of the most wonderful works of art that animation has delivered in years. It's also one of the fantasy movies with the most interesting characters, which is only one of the many reasons why it's an absolute must-see.

Who, if not Hayao Miyazaki, could be behind yet another one of the most ambitious fantasy movies ever made? It is, of course, Ghibli's Princess Mononoke, which is set in the Muromachi period of Japanese history. In it, a young prince cursed by a demon journeys into a war between an industrial mining town and the forest gods, who fight back alongside a girl raised by wolves.

It's one of the darkest, most violent, and most mature movies that Studio Ghibli have thus far made, and it also just so happens to arguably be the greatest low fantasy animated feature ever made. Though its world-building prioritizes historical realism over fantasy, there's still more than plenty of it to satisfy fans of the genre. An enrapturing story about the destructive cycle of hatred and ecological exploitation, it's easily one of the best outings in Miyazaki's filmography.

#3515. Missing 2-Year-Old Found After 7 Hours In Arizona Desert In Nothing But Her Diaper

A scary story had a happy ending in Arizona ... when a missing 2-year-old was found alive in the desert wearing nothing but a diaper ... 7 hours after she disappeared from home.

Search volunteer Jay Stewart found the missing toddler just after midnight Wednesday, about 2 miles from her Eloy home. She had been last seen in her yard around 5 PM.

He told ABC15 ... "To find that little scared child, the way she popped out of that bush, it was. I'll never forget it the rest as long as I live."

Video shows the moment Jay handed the little girl over to the cops after rescuing her ... and it's pretty heroic.

Pinal County Sheriff Ross Teeple says ... "This is a large family of kids. One of them walked away. Turns out she was a two-year-old child wearing nothing but a diaper. I mean, she didn't even have shoes on, guys."

Over 75 law enforcement officers across various agencies joined in the search for the terrified toddler, but Jay -- a neighbor -- was ultimately the one who found her.

He said ... "I leaned over looking under these bushes, thinking she might be laying down because it was cold."

Jay recalled ... "And when I leaned over one time, and I'm calling her name... and behind me to my left, I hear something that didn't even sound human. It was probably a relief, or fright, or whatever."

He said she'd been sitting in the dirt, adding ... "I grabbed her and picked her up, and then she was like clinging to me, so tight, so tight."

Teeple said they had to act fast because of the desert weather ... "It's Arizona. We're all familiar with the heat, but we forget in the wintertime that very remote areas like this can get extremely cold very fast."

He added ... "And she's a small body producing very little heat, so the drones with the heat signatures could not pick up anything. So this was people had to go out in foot and go out and search for the this young little girl."

The little girl was brought to the hospital as a precaution. The Department of Child Safety says it seems like the kid simply wandered off ... noting there were no indications of abuse.

#3513. You Can Try WhatsApp's New Disappearing Text Messages Early

Like Snapchat messages, WhatsApp's "View Once" feature is a great way to send things you don't want living on your friends' devices. You can send voice messages, photos, and videos that will "self-destruct" after they're opened, limiting (if not eliminating) the risk of your friends keeping them forever. However, View Once has a major limitation: While WhatsApp will let you send voice memos and images that way, you can't use it to send texts, meaning every one you send will live on (unless you unsend it yourself).

That's now changing. As reported by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is now beta testing View Once for text messages, too. Soon enough, you'll be able to send voice memos, photos, videos, and texts as one-time-only messages. That way, you can send sensitive information via text—say, a password or an important account number—without worrying about it persisting. Here's how it works: You craft your text message as you usually do, but rather than tap the send button, you hold it. You'll see the usual "Schedule message" option, but once the feature rolls out, you'll also find a new "View Once" option as well.

As mentioned above, this feature is currently in testing, so it's only available to WhatsApp beta testers. What's more, only the Android version of the beta has access at the moment, so iOS beta testers are out of luck. (That said, the WhatsApp iOS beta is perpetually full, so there's not much you could do even if WhatsApp made this test available on iPhone.)

If you have an Android device, you can enroll in the WhatsApp beta to try out "View Once" text messages today. According to WABetaInfo, the feature is live as of WhatsApp version 2.26.45.6. To enroll, open the WhatsApp beta page on the Google Play store and enroll your account in the beta. If you don't have WhatsApp on your phone already, download it here; if you do, reload the page and install the latest update. This will update your existing WhatsApp app to the latest beta version.

#3512. 'You Can See Everything' Studio A24 Will Pay Billy Evans Through Charitable Donation

Turns out "You Can See Everything," except the truth about whether the smash-hit documentary compensated its subjects -- Elizabeth Holmes and Billy Evans -- because the studio behind it really IS coughing up a lot of dough.

Sources with knowledge confirm to TMZ, A24 is making the controversial backend payment to a charity. At the end of the movie, a title card tells the audience, "Billy Evans ultimately relinquished his negotiated share of the film's profits and would not receive backend compensation."

Technically, that's true, but as first reported by The Hollywood Reporter ... Billy did pick the children's nonprofit that's getting the money. It's unclear how much money the undisclosed charity is getting, but it'll be a percentage of the profits, and so far, the documentary's grossed a whopping $89 million domestically.

The payment is one of the movie's central, and highly debated, plot points. Traditionally and ethically, filmmakers don't pay the subjects of a documentary because the money could influence what they say.

What is clear is that ethical duty not to pay falls squarely on the filmmakers -- in this case, A24 -- and not the subjects of a documentary.

If we're keeping it real, the title card at the end of 'See Everything' seems to absolve A24 of having paid Billy ... but it turns out it did compensate a charity.

#3511. Baldur's Gate 3: Shadowheart Officially Confirmed For 2027 Release

The arrival of Grand Theft Auto 6 has taken over most gaming discussion, but it wasn't too long ago that Baldur's Gate 3 was at the top of the pile. While it's no longer the center of every conversation, the game has proven to have legs, and its story is now set to be expanded next year.

Those waiting for a game expansion or Baldur's Gate 4 aren't likely to be in luck any time soon, as developer Larian Studios has moved on to a new project in the Divinity series instead. If you're open to returning to the world of the Forgotten Realms in a different medium, though, Shadowheart is getting the spotlight in a 2027 book.

Today, the official Titan Books X account announced Baldur's Gate 3: Shadowheart, a prequel novel set to release in May 2027. Rather than picking up where her story left off in the game (which could vary wildly depending on the playthrough), Baldur's Gate 3: Shadowheart dives into the cleric's past. If you've played through much of the game, you won't be surprised to learn that it focuses on her time as a devoted priestess of Shar, setting up a "brutal murder" for her to investigate.

The description also refers to the book as a "darkly sexy fantasy," so it sounds like it may be leaning more into the romantasy genre. On the other hand, the sexy part could simply refer to the allure of Shadowheart's personality. The book comes courtesy of Tasha Suri, the author of the Burning Kingdoms trilogy, which is more of a fantasy story that features romance than a full-on romantasy series.

Some Baldur's Gate 3 fans might receive the news of another book with a bit of trepidation, as the track record behind the idea is a bit controversial. Baldur's Gate 3: Astarion, which released recently, didn't go over particularly well with much of the community. Astarion's backstory touches on plenty of heavy topics, and the character's fans had plenty to say about how the book handled them.

Baldur's Gate 3: Shadowheart may also have to handle some loaded material, as Shadowheart has a dark backstory herself, although not in quite the same way as Astarion. With a different subject and a different author at the helm, though, it should still be on the radar of Baldur's Gate 3 fans. There's always a chance that it could deliver a meaningful narrative expansion to the game, although satisfying every Shadowheart lover would be a tall order.

Elsewhere in the realm of Baldur's Gate 3 tie-ins, a new comic series will be kicking off in February 2027, starting with an arc focused on Astarion that will hopefully go over more smoothly than the book did. And, of course, it's always possible for Dungeons & Dragons players to tell new Baldur's Gate 3 stories at the game table, giving the beloved game a chance to live forever in the hands of all of its fans.

#3509. I Tested Pangram to See If It Can Really Detect AI-Generated Content Like It Claims

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

We know it can be difficult for human beings to spot AI-generated content, but can detection software fare any better? Pangram is one of the leaders in the field, promising a "near-zero false positive rate" by looking at "subtle cues" in the writing, based on a training and feedback model comparing human-made content with the AI equivalent.

You'll find arguments on both sides of the debate as to whether or not Pangram's claims stand up. After a short story was flagged by Pangram and then judged to be free from AI, the detection engine has been accused of bias against text from minority writers.

Proponents of Pangram would point to an ongoing reward offer—currently at $3,950—available to anyone who can find a pre-2019 (and pre-LLM) piece of writing that Pangram falsely flags as being AI-written. So far, the reward is unclaimed.

As the AI detector has recently added AI image and video detection to its capabilities, it seemed a good time to put Pangram's analysis skills to the test for myself. Here's how it performed in the three different content types.

On the human side, I picked out 10 of my most recent articles for Lifehacker, known to be written by a person because I personally wrote them—in the traditional way, I fretted over word choices, went back and changed sentences, and accidentally left in a variety of typos that editors thankfully fixed.

For the AI content, I rotated between ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude, and got the LLMs to write 10 articles with the same headlines and the same approximate number of words, for a tech-savvy audience. I even asked the AI apps to vary their language use, so that the output would "read less like an LLM has written it."

Pangram's AI text detector lets you upload files, but to make the task a little harder, I copied and pasted all of the text into the online article, so it wouldn't be able to rely on any metadata included in the file. The scans got the correct result each and every time: Human-written text came back as 100% human, and AI-written text came back as 100% AI.

What's more, Pangram was certain about its results. All of the human writing was marked as highly likely to be human, and the vast majority of the AI writing was marked as highly likely to have come from an LLM. There were only a handful of phrases or sentences across thousands of AI words that got a "medium" rather than a "high" ranking for AI.

Now, there have been some edge cases where Pangram has got it wrong—like a poem repeating the same six words thousands of times—but as far as this sample goes, it can't be faulted. Clearly, my writing is too idiosyncratic and too clunky to be confused for the smooth sheen of AI-produced prose.

To be fair, I do have another advantage over AI: I can actually test out devices and apps in a way that LLM bots can't. ChatGPT can't experiment with One UI 9 (at least not yet), though it can scrape the web for various experiments and tests that real people have done.

However, I was able to fool Pangram to some extent by alternating AI paragraphs with human-written paragraphs. The text was flagged as AI, but the percentage estimate was typically lower (20-25%) than what it actually was (around 50%). If you're offloading some but not all of your writing to AI, some of it might slip though as real.

Image and video detection is the new string to Pangram's bow, so I sifted through my phone's photo and video library for some pieces of content to test the AI on. Again, I used copy and paste to get the files into Pangram rather than uploading them, to limit how much information the AI detector could get from metadata.

Again, all the human-made content was recognized as such, with a very high level of certainty—whether it was complicated crowd shots or simpler images of natural scenes. Presumably, there are even more signals to go off than there are with writing, including camera movements, colors, style, consistency, and composition.

Next up, I generated a few images and videos in Google Gemini and ChatGPT, requesting results that would look as photorealistic and "non-AI" as possible—the resulting files covered people, animals, and buildings. As before, I used copy, paste, and a few screengrabs to try and limit the metadata Pangram had access to.

Here, too, the AI identification was spot on, with all of the artificial content recognized as such, to a high level of confidence. This is perhaps not surprising: I think AI images and especially AI video still have more "tells" than AI writing, especially if you've seen a lot of it, so I wasn't expecting Pangram to fail here.

I did try experimenting with real photos that had a little bit of AI in them, what with tools like Gemini and ChatGPT now so good at image editing, as well as creating pictures from scratch. These were marked as "unsure" by Pangram, though to cut it some slack, only a small amount of the images were altered.

As with the text, the best way to beat Pangram's detection systems seems to be to include some AI embedded in human-made content. It will most likely still fail the "100% human" test, but the tests I ran showed that Pangram is less certain in these cases, or underestimates the amount of AI there actually is.

Increase the level of AI, and the detection gets more reliable—but if you're only using AI for a small part of whatever it is you're making, it's less worthwhile using AI tools anyway. As far as these tests go, Pangram's claims about accuracy check out, making it a useful tool if you need to ensure something is AI-free.
