#3422. ‘Josephine’ Will Floor You

This is the question that an eight-year-old named Josephine (Mason Reeves) asks her dad, Damien (Channing Tatum). She’s a sporty kid, the kind of youngster who accompanies her jockish pops on long runs through Golden Gate Park every Sunday morning. It’s during one of these weekly father-daughter bonding sessions that Josephine sprints ahead of her dad and strays off their usual path. Stopping to catch her breath, she sees a female jogger go into a public restroom at the bottom of a hill. Then Josephine watches as a stranger pulls the woman out, knocks her to the ground, and sexually assaults her.

The cops arrest the perpetrator, the survivor goes to the hospital, and eventually, Damien is left with his daughter and that question, hanging in the air. Josephine can’t comprehend what she’s witnessed. Her father doesn’t know how to answer. Instead of comforting or explaining, Damien just resumes their usual training exercises; he’s got to strengthen her up for soccer, he tells his daughter. His intentions are noble. He wants to protect her by pretending nothing’s happened. But Josephine’s father is simply the first adult who fails to help her process the traumatic experience this young girl has gone through. He won’t be the last.

The Grand Jury Prize winner at this year’s Sundance Film Festival, Josephine doesn’t just follow its namesake as she’s forced to navigate a sudden loss of innocence; it sticks so closely to her perspective that you’re allowed to see every confusing gesture, every mixed-message reply, every argument among her parents, and every acting-out response through her eyes. That itself isn’t unusual — most coming-of-age movies let you walk miles in their hero’s Converse All Stars. Yet writer-director Beth de Araújo’s sophomore film handles this shattering take on a kid wrapping her head around trauma with such grace, such delicacy, such force and a lack of false notes, that the work feels seismic even in its silences. It’s not interested in debating how crimes are handled by the cops or the courts, or how society talks around instead of about sexual violence in a constructive way. The movie wants you to reckon with the impact of someone figuring out a foreign landscape filled with unforeseen terrors. Josephine, c’est moi. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

So much of this rests on the tiny shoulders of Reeves, a first-time actor who seems to intuitively understand how to simply be in front of the camera. When Araújo isn’t replicating Josephine’s point of view, letting things unfold from a lower angle looking up or glimpsed from a distance, she’s training her lens directly on Reeves’ face in close-up. You can see the character attempting to grasp and contextualize situations for which she has no reference point in real time. And when Josephine begins to parrot statements and repeat patterns of behavior — she sees Damien spit on the rapist, then later spits on her dad in a fit of rage — we can see her trying on toxic versions of adulthood for size. It’s an incredible performance by any parameter, much less one delivered by a preteen.

Josephine makes space for her parents as well, with Tatum weaponizing his varsity-athlete physicality and kinder, gentler masculinity to play Damien as a well-meaning yet grasping dad, a paterfamilias in over his head when it comes to talking about tough subjects. His solutions: Take a self-defense class and either sweat out the pain or bury it. Gemma Chan plays Josephine’s mom, a dancer named Claire, as someone both more sympathetic to their child’s bewilderment and equally adrift. (A sequence in which she’s asked by her daughter if she’s ever been assaulted is all the more painful by the lack of an actual answer; Chan’s look alone tells you more than you feel you should know.) Tempers get lost, voices get raised, and Josephine herself lashes out in ways that suggest she doesn’t know how to deal with the emotional turbulence coursing through her. There’s a scene that takes place in a partially painted nursery that you may require you to cover your eyes. Trending Stories Marlon Jackson Reveals Stage 4 Prostate Cancer Diagnosis Selena Gomez Shares Her Reaction to Martin Short Ruining Her Wedding Cake Some Gamers Are Pissed That ‘GTA VI’ Makes Them Be Nice to Their Girlfriend Trump Got Played by Putin and Xi Related Content How a 1972 Cocktail Party Gave Us the Best Documentary of the Year Channing Tatum Says He Hasn’t Been Harassing Zoë Kravitz and Harry Styles With Burner Account ‘The Weight’ Isn’t a Perfect Homage to 1970s Tough-Guy Movies. But It’s Close ‘I Want Your Sex’ Works Out the Kinks of a BDSM Relationship

You don’t need to know that Josephine comes from an extremely personal place to feel that Araújo (whose debut, a Neo-Nazi Karen parable titled Soft and Quiet, now feels like an artist clearing her throat before speaking harshly and loudly) is unpacking this youngster’s story with an extraordinary amount of acuity and sensitivity, even as she refuses to pull punches: The assault is shown forensically, pitilessly, and in full. So is Josephine’s cross-examination on the stand by the defense’s lawyer (Dana Millican) when the child is forced to testify as a witness, which represents the ways our legal system can put everyone involved on trial. Surreal touches, such as the ghostly presence of the rapist (Philip Ettinger) hovering around everyday situations, add to the feeling that you’re viewing all of this through a highly subjective lens. Josephine sees this person everywhere, as a phantom both menacing and eerily childlike. So why shouldn’t we?

“Do you think the man is bad on the inside?” Josephine asks one of her caretakers. “Or good on the inside, but does bad things?” Nobody really knows the answer to that, she’s told. Neither Araújo nor the movie itself pretends to have a satisfying reply. But it’s desperate to ask the question and push you to wonder how a child, in some ways wise beyond her years yet still very much a kid, can reckon with a morality that exists in deepening shades of gray. Josephine is a movie that begins in a moment of fear — Josephine is scared to run out of her garage before the automatic door closes — and ends with a portrait of courage under fire. That the courage comes from someone who can barely comprehend her own bravery only makes the moment that much more impressive. It’s hard to think of a work of art that feels this simultaneously scarring and healing. Or that is tougher to watch yet something that must be seen as soon as possible and by any means necessary.

#3421. When Electric Cars Were for Women

Early carmakers decided women wanted cars that were quiet, clean, and easy to start

Allison Marsh is a professor at the University of South Carolina and the codirector of the Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society.

When automobiles were still a novelty, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion.

At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.

Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.

Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.

In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.

The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.

I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.

This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens

According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.

Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.

While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).

Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens

Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.

When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.

Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)

Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.

Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

References For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.

Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

Allison Marsh is a professor in Women and Gender Studies at the University of South Carolina and codirector of the university’s Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society. She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.

#3420. iFixit tears down Apple HomeView, finds lots of glue and endless frustration

iFixit’s teardown of the new Apple HomeView is now up, revealing a device that seems nearly impossible to take apart and repair. Watch it below.

Following last week’s launch of the Apple HomeView, iFixit today published its teardown of the device.

Contrary to recent teardowns, which found significant repairability improvements with greater component modularity and easier access to internal components, the HomeView put up a fight nearly all the way through.

With heavily glued or adhesive-bonded components, including the display, speakers, antennas, and logic board, the teardown proved particularly challenging, even after the adhesive securing the display’s speakers was soaked in isopropyl alcohol.

At one point, one of them broke apart during removal, while the logic board required considerable force to separate from the chassis due to the thermal adhesive holding it in place.

iFixit’s teardown covered the two HomeView variants: the tabletop model and the wall-mounted version. Interestingly, there are some internal differences between them, as the wall-mounted model has a slightly wider logic board to accommodate capacitors that are housed in the base of the tabletop version.

As a result, the wall-mounted HomeView also has smaller internal speakers, which helps explain the differences in their audio systems that Apple had already acknowledged at launch.

Back to the tabletop model, iFixit’s teardown also showed that separating the display from the base requires either specialized tools or extensive, potentially destructive disassembly of the display assembly, thanks to the way Apple routed the connecting cables through the pivot mechanism.

Once iFixit was in the base, however, there was some good news: the USB-C port is modular and relatively easy to access, as are the passive radiators and the board powering the lower assembly.

Still, an extremely short cable connecting the woofer to the board underneath made disassembly difficult, with iFixit questioning how anyone would be able to reconnect it during reassembly.

Percentage of Apple owners who are interested in repairing their device. 0.000001%

Percentage of Apple owners who will actually try and repair their device. 0.00000001%

Given all these repairability challenges, Shahram Mokhtari joked that while iFixit doesn’t have an official repairability scorecard for this category of device, he would give the Apple HomeView a “BEEP this thing” out of 10.

To check out iFixit’s blog post, which features an interactive 3D CT scan of the HomeView, follow this link.

Be sure to also catch 9to5Mac’s review of the Apple HomeView.

D’Angelo’s music being posthumously immortalized in the most anticipated video game in a decade is a fitting tribute to the singer, given his previous collaborations with Rockstar Games, the company behind GTA VI. “[D’Angelo] would come in here [Rockstar’s New York city office] and just play the game. #3415. Apple announces App Store price changes in multiple countries, new California tax rules

Apple today announced that App Store prices for apps and In-App Purchases will be adjusted in five countries starting December 3, following changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates. Here are the details.

In a new post published on its developer portal, Apple today announced a series of changes to App Store pricing, as well as updates to tax rules affecting developers and customers in several countries, including the US.

According to the company, developers’ proceeds from eligible app and In-App Purchase sales have been adjusted in four countries, reflecting the following tax updates:

Specific to Botswana and Rwanda, Apple said that “Exhibit B of the Paid Applications Agreement will be updated to indicate that Apple collects and remits applicable taxes.”

Apple added that a new “Software as a Service (SaaS)” attribute is now available for several App Store tax categories, including App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting. Developers can review and update their tax category selections in App Store Connect.

Additionally, starting December 3, developers who rely on Apple’s automatic pricing adjustments will see changes to app and In-App Purchase prices in:

Apple usually makes these adjustments to account for changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates, and notes that prices won’t change in countries selected as the base storefront, for auto-renewable subscriptions, or in storefronts where developers manually manage their prices.

The announcement does not go into detail about how much prices will change in each country, or whether they will increase or decrease.

Finally, starting January 1, 2027, apps and In-App Purchases in the SaaS, App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting categories will become subject to sales and use taxes in California.

Apple noted that “prices on the United States storefront are displayed to customers exclusive of taxes, so the tax change will not affect them,” but added that while developers’ proceeds will remain unchanged, “the total amount customers are charged, inclusive of tax, may increase.”

#3412. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

#3411. The UK and some other countries don’t get more Siri AI usage with iCloud+

Apple this week revealed the additional Siri AI usage you’ll get if you have an iCloud+ subscription. This ranges from doubled limits for a 200GB plan to 20 times for a 12TB plan.

However, the company’s support document reveals that some countries will not get access to these increased usage allowances …

Apple hasn’t yet specified the standard limits applicable to Siri AI usage, instead saying that these will vary depending on anything from the feature used to the overall level of demand at the time. However, it did list the proportional increases you get with paid iCloud plans.

However, tucked away in the small print in the company’s support document are some exclusions. One of them is no surprise: EU countries.

Siri AI isn’t available at all in the EU due to Apple’s perception of potential antitrust issues. Essentially, Apple believes that if it launches Siri AI there, it will be required to give competing AI services the same level of access to its devices. But three other countries are specifically excluded:

Apple gives no explanation, simply saying:

Increased access to Siri AI with iCloud+ is subject to Siri AI availability and is not available in Brazil, the EU, UK, or South Korea.

However, I have a strong suspicion about the reason.

What all three countries have in common is that they’ve taken a strong antitrust stance with Apple on a number of occasions over a range of issues.

It may be that Apple has genuine concerns about how regulators might respond if they effectively throw in free access to increased Siri AI usage. The company may fear that this would be viewed as anti-competitive by implicitly disadvantaging other AI services.

A less charitable take would be that Apple is firing a warning shot across the bows of these countries, seeking to communicate that there are consequences for what it views as attacks on its ecosystem. If customers are angered by missing out, Apple might be hoping that these feelings would be directed at regulators rather than the iPhone maker.

What’s your take? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

Rune Factory Guardians of Azuma is my favorite Nintendo Switch 2 game so far. It delivers a little bit of everything I love: exciting action-RPG combat, satisfying farming mechanics, a great story and a memorable cast of characters you can get to know. Plus, for the first time in the series you can place buildings and decorations to encourage more people to move into the villages you oversee.

It's a game that packs a lot in, but each aspect of the gameplay is balanced perfectly. And it provides dozens of hours of content, so it's great value — especially with this discount.

The Switch version is also on sale for $19, if you want to save even more.

Whenever I'm playing my Nintendo Switch 2 in docked mode, the GameSir Super Nova is the controller I reach for. And I'm not the only one who loves it — it made our list of the best Nintendo Switch 2 controllers as the best option on a budget.

Not only does it cost half the price of the Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller, it offers features that Nintendo's controllers don't, like Hall Effect triggers and thumbsticks. It's a comfortable, lightweight controller that won't succumb to the dreaded stick drift (like the Joy-Cons on my original Nintendo Switch console did.)

Yes, several third-party accessories and games are already on sale; most of those aren't Nintendo-made.

My colleague looked through the PlayStation Black Friday sale for five deals that are worth your money.

So, earlier I said I didn't think The Legend of Zelda Ocarina of Time would be discounted for Black Friday. Now I'm eating those words, because the game is $5 off right now at Amazon. It's a small discount, but it's a greatly appreciated one. This game only just released, after all! The discount is on a digital version of the game from Amazon. Grab it before it disappears!

If you've already got The Legend of Zelda Ocarina of Time, the next thing you should do is outfit yourself with some Zelda gear. Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda merch page has a bunch of Zelda tees and hoodies on sale, starting from just $15. There are several design options available and you can also choose the color of the tee you want in most cases.

From Tarsier Studios, the team behind Little Nightmares, comes this chilling horror game. It can be played in single player or co-op — and I highly recommend bringing a friend along for this one, because it might be too scary to play alone.

In his Reanimal review, our Senior Entertainment Editor Rory Mellon wrote: "Reanimal might be the spookiest game I’ve played in months. The game’s compelling combination of atmospheric, shadow-blanketed locations and horrific, warped creatures that relentlessly hunt you down had my heart rate quickening right from the start."

The Samsung S90F is the best gaming TV we've tested. The 77-inch model was originally priced at $3,499 at launch (ouch) but now, Amazon is selling it for $1,847. That's a discount of $1,752, almost half off compared to the launch price!

It's still an expensive TV for sure, but you get a massive 77-inch display with near-perfect contrast according to our tests — as well as rich colors and wide viewing angles. You also get access to Gaming Hub, which lets you tweak the picture settings for your games to perfection; and the lag time is extremely low at just 9.1ms.

I think everybody should give the Ace Attorney games a shot, so I can't not include this deal in this live blog. In this visual novel game series, you play as a lawyer and must question witnesses, use evidence and solve puzzles to prove your clients innocent! The games are packed with extremely memorable and loveable characters, hilarious dialogue and tough legal cases to untangle.

This collection includes three games: Apollo Justice Ace Attorney, Dual Destinies, and Spirit of Justice. There are also bonus goodies for fans, like special extra episodes and an art gallery.

Earlier, I posted about a Switch charging case that can juice up your console on the move. The case is convenient, but not the cheapest way to get extra power. So if you're looking for a more affordable — and more pocketable — solution, this Iniu 10,000mAh power bank is one of the best we've tested, and it's barely any larger than an AirPods case. The 45W speed means it charges fast, too. It's just a hair above its lowest price ever of $26 right now.

Sonic x Shadow Generations, one of our favorite games on the Switch, is currently 60% off, so you can get it for just $19 at Amazon.

This 2-in-1 game combines a remaster of 2011's Sonic Generations, a love letter to the Blue Blur that remains a fan-favorite to this day, with a new Shadow-focused campaign. It's a strong package overall and even better on sale for a discount.

Untitled Goose Game is one of the best Switch games of all time and I’ll die on this hill. Right now, you can grab the game for 60% off at the Nintendo Store!

You play as a goose going around an unsuspecting village and pulling pranks on the residents. There are five main areas and you're given quest items to check off. You'll be asked to steal a boy's glasses, make the gardener wear his sun hat, make a man spit out his tea, among other things. How you achieve these is entirely up to you.

Want more couch co-op game recommendations? We’ve got you covered!

Overcooked! and Overcooked! 2 are two of our favorite couch co-op games, and right now, you can grab the All You Can Eat Edition (which includes both) for just $32. In this cartoon cooking simulator, you and up to three other players must cook and deliver dishes in quick succession — the quicker you are, the more tips you earn.

Chop, dice, slice, steam, fry, bake, rinse and repeat — and don't forget to wash those dishes and put out the fires lest they burn your kitchen down. Each level lasts only a few minutes, and you'll keep coming back for more!

Have you heard of a little game called GTA 6 that just launched and quickly became the most acclaimed video game in history? While it isn't on the Switch, you don't have to feel left out. Instead, you can grab the GTA The Trilogy Definitive Edition for just $32 at Amazon. Three games for the price of one? Yes please!

The Trilogy includes GTA III which takes place in Liberty City; GTA Vice City; and GTA San Andreas where you play as CJ. This three-in-one pack will keep you busy for a while.

Cyberpunk 2077 had a messy release back in 2022. But that was a long time ago, and the devs have done their due diligence and cleaned up the game a lot since then. We now rank it as one of the best Nintendo Switch 2 games for its extremely memorable setting and atmosphere, as well as its enjoyable quests. And Keanu Reeves and Idris Elba both star as major characters — that's another big draw!

The Belkin Charging Case for Nintendo Switch 2 is a smart buy if you want an easy way to keep your Switch 2 juiced up on the go. It comes with a case and a 10,000mAh power bank that'll charge up your Switch 2 console 1.5 times over — enough to get you five hours of playtime in total (or more, if you're playing less graphically intense titles.) That definitely comes in handy for longer commutes or short-haul flights.

Note: it's possible to buy a Switch 2 case and a 10,000mAh power bank separately for less than $59. But with this deal, you get everything in one convenient package, which makes traveling easier.

Earlier, I shared a deal on the $14 Turtle Beach Airlite Fit. They're excellent for the price, but they're wired headphones. If you want a wireless pair, the SteelSeries Arctis Nova 3 are a worthy pick!

They made our list of the best gaming headsets as the best PC headset, but they're very good for Switch gamers too. If you don't mind the plasticy build, they deliver immersive sound, a comfortable fit and a great mic. Oh, and the Aqua and Lavender color options look great, too.

Mario + Rabbids is one of the cheapest games you'll find that stars Mario and friends — and it's also an underrated gem. This tactical RPG looks colorful and cuddly, but requires some serious strategy, especially if you want to beat the toughest levels. There's also a sequel, Sparks of Hope, that we gave 4 stars to in our review. If you want a super affordable game with lots of content, either of these titles will serve you well.

We're a week out from Black Friday now, and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is still priced at $69. Will it go on sale for Black Friday? I can't predict what will happen, but I honestly don't think it will be discounted. It's a brand new first-party Nintendo game and those don't often see discounts right after release. I would grab it now so you can spend an extra week enjoying this GOTY nominee over the holiday season! However, if you did want to wait and see, I wouldn't blame you for making that choice either.

If you loved Donkey Kong Bananza (us too!) and want to monkey around even more — or don't have a Switch 2 yet, but don't want to miss all the fun — Donkey Kong Country Returns HD is the game you should play next. It's an excellent 2D platformer with challenging levels, great music and a huge stash of hidden bananas to collect. We also rank it as one of the best Nintendo Switch multiplayer games.

A screen protector can save your Switch 2 from scratches, scuffs and fingerprints — things most people want to avoid. This deal gets you a set of two glass screen protectors from Next, with reviewers saying they're easy to install and use. While we haven't tested these exact ones at TG, the 4.6-star rating gives me confidence they won't fail you.

On November 22, the Nintendo Switch 2 Mario Kart World bundle will drop from $549 to $499. That's $50 off and a total saving of $87 compared to buying the bundled items individually. This deal is just two days away and it's so close, I can almost taste it! If you're hoping to get your hands on it, I recommend doing so ASAP once the 22nd is here. I think the deal could sell out in a flash.

If you just can't wait, you can get the Nintendo Switch 2 Mario Kart World bundle for $549 right now and save $37.

This is a deal worth noting for Switch fans! This Animal Crossing Lego set is retired according to the Lego website, and Amazon is selling it with a massive 51% discount. I rarely see Lego discounts this big! Aside from that, it's an awesome set that represents the Animal Crossing game series very well, with two houses, three animal friends and foliage that shows the changing seasons.

Still haven't jumped into the Xenoblade series? You're in for a treat. Years back, we recommended Xenoblade Chronicles Definitive Edition as one of the first games you should play on your new Nintendo Switch, and it's just as essential today. Featuring unique action-RPG combat, a truly gargantuan world to explore and a deep, engaging story, it's one of the best games in the genre for sure.

Cult of the Lamb: Definitive Edition is on sale for Black Friday! (The base game is also available for $24 at Nintendo.) This game is the perfect mix of cute and creepy — you'll need to gather animal friends, collect supplies to keep them happy and healthy and decorate your living area... oh, and fight horrific monsters and make sacrifices.

Kirby and the Forgotten Land is packed with simple fun. Playing as Kirby, you can swallow enemies to gain new abilities and traverse a lush, overgrown urban wasteland — a unique setting for a Nintendo game.

Like most Kirby games, the stages aren't too difficult to clear, so the challenge comes from combing back over levels to look for hidden secrets and collectables. That makes it great for kids and adults alike, whether they're experienced gamers or not. Oh, and since there's the option for co-op multiplayer, both kinds of gamers can team up and play together at the same time.

I just posted about a deal on Metroid Dread, and it's a game that benefits highly from playing with a good pair of headphones. Not only will great sound help you get fully immersed, it'll help you play better too — audio cues can be vitally important, depending on what you're playing.

The Turtle Beach Airlite Fit have been on sale at this price for a couple of days now, and I honestly can't believe they haven't sold out. They're one of the best gaming headsets we've tested, particularly for Nintendo Switch gamers, and offer sound quality and features that are way better than you'd expect considering their tiny price tag. Grab a pair and all your games will sound better!

Here's a Black Friday headliner! Several of Nintendo's biggest hitters are discounted today with 30% off. While we'll have to wait a little longer for those exciting physical game discounts, you can save 30% on a couple of huge Nintendo Switch titles in digital form right now.

#3409. There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication issues." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

That pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen."

But to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

Love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering new security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

Mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find new security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be said for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

You might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October update. The company's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

It's important to understand that just about every company that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as quickly as possible.

The implications aren't specific to any one company, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

Of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

#3408. Banks, FAA, Microsoft, Apple – no systemic attack on the US, says White House

A set of major tech outages in close succession is leading some to speculate that they are connected, and that the US is under systemic attack by a hostile state.

All the evidence suggests otherwise, with individual explanations for each of them – and the White House is now saying as much in a bid to put fears to rest …

Whether there was or wasn't a cyber attack, I wouldn't believe a single word from the White House.

On Thursday, a widespread Microsoft 365 outage ran into the following day when two unrelated issues coincided. Friday saw a nationwide ground stop of US air traffic due to a communication issue affecting all air traffic control centers. On Monday, a bug in a Chase bank system saw disruption not only to the bank itself, but also other banks where Chase was a party to a transaction. Finally, yesterday saw many Apple services offline, with retail stores also affected.

The Apple outage doesn’t appear to have been significant enough to have reached the administration’s radar, but CBS News reports secretary of state Marco Rubio saying the others are unrelated.

“The Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago. These issues that we’ve seen from a technical standpoint are completely unrelated one from another,” Rubio said […]

“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind. Each of them are distinct, and they’re different in their causation.”

The statement was backed by Senator Mark Warner.

Democratic Sen. Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, also said on Tuesday that there’s no indication these incidents are the result of an attack.

Warner went on to say that the ability of AI systems to find vulnerabilities at “unprecedented speed” does, however, mean companies and government agencies alike need to be ready to patch vulnerabilities immediately.

#3407. Megan Moroney and Alex Warren Know a Good Song When They Hear It in the Car

For country chart-topper Megan Moroney and pop hitmaker Alex Warren, a song isn’t necessarily finished when it leaves the studio. Sometimes, it needs a test drive.

For Warren, listening to music in the car holds sentimental meaning. On his new album, Wildchild, he pays tribute to his late father, who died of cancer when Warren was just nine years old. Some of his most powerful musical memories with his dad are inseparable from time spent in the car.

“My only memory of music growing up was getting in the car and listening to my dad’s CDs, and John Mayer was his guy,” Warren said. “When my dad passed away, I got in his car and [Mayer’s album] came on. When I wrote this song for my dad called ‘Wildchild,’ I put his voice on it, and I asked [Mayer] to do a guitar solo on it, so my dad and John have a song.”

The car is also where Warren discovered Moroney’s music. He recalls listening to her breakout hit “Tennessee Orange” in the car with his wife, who knew every word.

“She knows that song like the back of her hand, and it’s really cool because she applies it to her own life,” Warren said of Moroney’s autobiographical debut, which tells the story of a die-hard Georgia football fan falling for a Tennessee Volunteers fan.

“It encapsulates the kind of music my fans like,” said Moroney, whose sharp-eyed songwriting turns specific details into universal feelings that resonate with the masses.

“It’s creative, it’s honest, there’s the hook, and it’s storytelling. I feel like at the root of all of my songs, that’s what it is. And obviously I’m a Georgia Bulldog, so it’s just very me.”

Moroney and Warren may come from different corners of the music world, but the two found plenty of common ground during a conversation outside Fox & Locke, a storied live-music venue tucked into the rolling countryside of Leiper’s Fork, Tennessee. The discussion was part of Rolling Stone’s Musicians on Musicians series. This time, Lexus sought to connect two artists from different backgrounds in an entirely new way by trading the usual lounge-like venues that host Musicians on Musicians conversations for the lounge-inspired quiet cabin of an all-electric 2027 Lexus TZ, which will make its debut this winter. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

As the conversation continued, Moroney and Warren learned that their paths to stardom have more than a few parallels. Both got an early boost from TikTok before breaking through with massive singles from their debut albums — Moroney with her five-times-platinum “Tennessee Orange,” Warren with his record-breaking “Ordinary.” Both have crossed genre lines through collaborations, and both released hit albums this year: Moroney’s autobiographical Cloud 9 and Warren’s deeply personal Wildchild. They also share a belief in one essential part of the creative process: the all-important “car test.”

For Warren, that test played a pivotal role in one of the biggest songs of his career. After receiving an early, stripped-down version of “Ordinary” — little more than his voice and a piano — he played it for his wife while they were driving. Her reaction told him everything he needed to know. “She was like, ‘I want more of it!’”

The experience changed the way he shares new music. “Now I only show people songs in my car.”

He might be onto something. Whether you’re a professional musician or more of a carpool-karaoke type, there’s something about hearing a song on the road that changes the experience. A lyric lands a little harder. A melody feels a little bigger. And sometimes, the right song at the right moment can turn a daily drive into something worth remembering. Cosmetics’ ‘Mirror Mix’

It helps when the sound system is up to the task. The all-electric Lexus TZ features an available 21-speaker Mark Levinson audio system, engineered specifically for the TZ’s three-row cabin to deliver the kind of rich, immersive sound that feels the way it was meant to be heard.

Of course, when your life revolves around music, sometimes the best soundtrack is no soundtrack at all. For artists like Moroney and Warren, who spend much of their time on the road, a long drive can also offer a rare chance to unplug, catch up, and simply have a conversation. Trending Stories Marlon Jackson Reveals Stage 4 Prostate Cancer Diagnosis Selena Gomez Shares Her Reaction to Martin Short Ruining Her Wedding Cake Some Gamers Are Pissed That ‘GTA VI’ Makes Them Be Nice to Their Girlfriend Trump Got Played by Putin and Xi

The TZ makes room for both experiences, and that balance between sound and silence feels particularly fitting for two artists who know a song’s power to make a personal story resonate far beyond its original inspiration.

It’s a reminder that the songs we carry with us are rarely just about the music. They’re tied to people, places, and moments that stick around long after the last note fades. And sometimes, the best way to know whether a song really works is to get behind the wheel, turn it up, and see where it takes you.

#3406. IEEE Computer Society Chapter Offers Webinars With Industry Experts

Attendees in Region 4 learn about AI, cybersecurity, and more

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and secretary of the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter.

To help engineers keep up with emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, and sustainable infrastructure, and learn how they can be applied in practice, the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter recently launched its Tech Talk Series.

The live webinar series connects IEEE members, undergrad and graduate students, and engineering professionals from IEEE Region 4 with industry practitioners. The monthly sessions have covered AI governance and security, agentic systems, and related topics. The sessions featured speakers from Apple, software company Tavant, and cybersecurity concern Zscaler.

Upcoming sessions and registration details are available on the IEEE Region 4 virtual events calendar.

Rather than presenting on emerging technologies only at a conceptual level, speakers discussed the design decisions behind specific tools and systems, how the systems are structured, and implementation challenges. They also shared lessons learned from using the tools in their daily work.

Sessions also include technical walkthroughs and practical examples.

The live format allows attendees to discuss and compare their approaches when evaluating and implementing new technologies with those used by other organizations.

The organizers chose to make the series virtual so that chapter members and other attendees could participate in technical discussions with engineers from major technology companies and eliminate the need to travel.

For young professionals, the sessions connect what they’ve learned in a classroom with the realities of the workplace.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. For experienced professionals, the talks offer a forum to examine new ways of designing, securing, and operating software systems, and compare technical approaches. They can ask questions relevant to systems being evaluated or deployed within their organization.

The most recent webinar, Feeding and Fencing AI Agents: Engineering Governed Agentic Systems on Real-Time Data, featured Gajendra Babu Thokala, a senior engineering leader at Apple in Seattle.

The IEEE senior member explained how teams can move beyond adding isolated AI features to applications and instead build governed AI-agent systems that use real-time business data to complete multistep business workflows.

Another recent session, Building AI Native Products: A Playbook for Agentic Systems, explored how products built around AI agents differ from traditional software. It also covered how agentic systems can help users complete multistep tasks and workflows. IEEE Senior Member Sandeep Shivam, a product and technology leader at Tavant in Dallas, led the webinar.

Those two sessions illustrate the series’ purpose: helping participants understand what a technology can do and what is required to use it responsibly.

Future sessions are being planned on areas including enterprise AI, software reliability, and responsible AI usage. In addition to speakers from technology companies, the chapter also plans to invite speakers from startups, universities, and research organizations.

Upcoming sessions are expected to cover cloud platforms, enterprise integrations, and the responsible development of AI systems.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Undergraduate and graduate students are invited to participate to gain exposure to technical decision-making and challenges encountered in professional engineering environments.

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and the secretary of the IEEE Computer Society Central Indiana Chapter. He is also the chair of the IEEE Central Indiana Student Activities Committee.

#3404. MacPaw’s Moonlock comes to iPhone, helping users detect potential scams

After launching Moonlock for Mac last year, MacPaw is bringing its scam-detection app to iPhone today. Here are the details.

When MacPaw launched Moonlock on the Mac, the company described its new app as something that “complements Apple’s built-in security tools, protects from Mac-specific malware, and helps you understand cybersecurity better.”

In practice, the Mac app includes real-time protection against potential threats. Users can also manually scan their Mac for malware, including suspicious files hidden in system folders and email attachments.

Beyond that, Moonlock includes a VPN to encrypt internet traffic, a network inspector that shows where apps are sending data and lets users block connections to specific countries, and an AI-powered scam detector that analyzes messages pasted into the app for signs of phishing. It also helps users review and adjust macOS security settings.

Today, MacPaw is launching Moonlock for iPhone, a move the company says “helps people recognize potential scams, understand their iPhone’s security and take practical steps to improve it.”

Unlike the Mac version, Moonlock for iPhone doesn’t scan for malware, as iOS prevents third-party apps from accessing other apps and their files. Instead, it focuses on identifying potential scams, checking for exposed personal information, and helping users improve their iPhone’s security.

On the iPhone, Moonlock lets users quickly check suspicious texts, screenshots, and QR codes for phishing, in addition to checking whether their email addresses have appeared in known data breaches.

As MacPaw explains it, Moonlock’s Scam Detect “helps people check suspicious messages they encounter throughout the day. Whether it’s a text message, a screenshot shared by a friend, or a QR code, users can paste, scan or share content directly with Moonlock and receive an assessment explaining why something may be suspicious.”

Here’s Oleg Stukalenko, Head of Product Management at Moonlock by MacPaw, on today’s launch:

“When we launched Moonlock, our goal was to make cybersecurity something anyone could understand and use. But so much of what people do today, from banking to everyday conversations, happens on their phones. Bringing Moonlock to iPhone felt like the natural next step. We want to help people spot a scam before they tap, see where their security stands, and know exactly what to do next.”
